694.title: How to keep reading
694.hook: you've read Genesis, Exodus, Psalms, the prophets, two gospels and three letters
694.howItsDone: Many Christians read the Bible through a church lectionary, a yearly reading plan, or slow prayerful reading such as lectio divina, often in a small group or alongside their congregation's Sunday readings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two short notes from the elder, and your line was face to face. Who did you see in person instead of on a screen? Day six hundred ninety-four.

Look at what you've read this year. Genesis, from the garden to Joseph's tears. Exodus, from the brick kilns to the mountain. The Psalms and the wisdom books. The prophets, with their burning coal and their valley of dry bones. Luke, start to finish. John, start to finish. Philippians, James, and the letters of the elder. That's a big piece of a big book. And it raises an honest question that comes up at exactly this point: when the lessons stop walking you through it, how do you keep reading?
screen: `A BIG PIECE OF A BIG BOOK.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. Bible comes from the Greek ta biblia, which means the books. Plural. It isn't one book; it's a library, written over many centuries in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek: poems, laws, letters, stories, songs and visions. Churches even shelve it a little differently. Protestant Bibles usually have sixty-six books, Catholic Bibles seventy-three, and Orthodox Bibles a few more. So the first tip is the one every library teaches: you don't have to read the shelves in order. Christians have found many ways in. Some follow a lectionary, a set of readings for each day or each Sunday, so a whole congregation hears the same passage the same week. Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and many other churches use one. Some follow a reading plan, a few chapters a day, through the whole Bible in a year. And some read very slowly. For centuries, monks have practiced lectio divina, holy reading: a short passage, read again and again, until one word catches and stays. The second tip: read with someone. The first churches heard these books read aloud, together; most people couldn't own a copy. A friend, a group, a church study, even one person who texts you a verse each morning keeps the book open. And the third: expect it to keep surprising you. A psalm read at twenty reads differently at fifty. Here is a verse from Psalm 119, in the King James Bible: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path." A lamp for your feet, not a floodlight for the whole road. Enough light for the next step, and then the next.
screen: `A LECTIONARY, A PLAN, A SLOW PAGE.`
then, large: `A LIGHT UNTO MY PATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose your next book. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the year. Which part pulled at you? If you loved the stories, you might try Acts, the story of the first churches, or Ruth, just four short chapters. If the Psalms spoke to you, you could keep one psalm a day. If you want more of Jesus, Mark is short and fast, and Matthew holds the Sermon on the Mount. Don't pick the hardest one. Pick the one you'll actually open. Then picture where and when: a chair, a time of day, a lamp. If you pray, you can ask for an open heart as you read. The bell holds the time.
How to keep reading. A library, not a single book: a lectionary, a plan or one slow page, ideally with someone beside you.
Your line: the book keeps opening. Today, read the first few verses of the book you chose, and stop where something catches. Day six hundred ninety-four.

695.title: Christmas: the Word again (John 1:14)
695.hook: at Christmas, churches read John's prologue: the Word became flesh
695.tomorrow: Year two close: the book in your hands
695.howItsDone: In Catholic, Anglican and many Protestant churches, John 1:1–14 is read on Christmas Day and often as the last lesson at services of lessons and carols; Orthodox churches read Matthew's account of the Magi at the Nativity and John's prologue at Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, how to keep reading, and your line was the book keeps opening. Which book did you choose, and what caught you? Day six hundred ninety-five.

Two Christmas readings, and they could hardly be more different. One is from Luke: shepherds, a manger, angels over the fields at night. The other is from John, and it has no manger at all. No shepherds, no star, no inn. It starts before time: in the beginning was the Word. In many churches, Luke's story is read at night, and John's opening is read on Christmas morning, or as the last reading at a candlelit service of lessons and carols. You read both Gospels this year. Today we come back to one verse in John, the one that makes it a Christmas text.

John's Gospel opens the way Genesis does. In the King James Bible: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." The Word, in Greek the logos: speech, reason, the meaning behind everything. Then: "And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not." And then the verse the whole passage leans toward, verse fourteen: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth." You met this verse in the autumn, through its tent: dwelt, in Greek, is pitched his tent. At Christmas, churches lean on the other word. Flesh. In Greek, sarx, the plain word for the stuff of bodies. John could have said the Word appeared, or visited. He says it became flesh. Not an idea, not a voice from the sky. At Christmas that flesh is a baby: someone who has to be fed, changed, carried and kept warm. Christians say the Word that was there in the beginning started out that small. Churches keep the day a little differently. Many celebrate on December twenty-fifth; many Orthodox churches that follow the older Julian calendar celebrate on what is now January seventh. Catholic, Anglican and many Protestant churches read this prologue on Christmas Day. In the Orthodox liturgy for the Nativity, the Gospel is Matthew's story of the Magi, and John's prologue is read at Easter instead. Same verse, same wonder, different places in the year. Luke tells you where he was born. John tells you who was born.
screen: `A BABY WHO HAS TO BE FED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read John 1:1–14 by a light. If you can, turn the room lights down and light one lamp or candle, safely. Settle, and breathe. Open to the first chapter of John and read the first fourteen verses slowly, out loud if you like. When you reach the light shining in the darkness, look at the flame for one breath. When you reach the Word made flesh, think of one ordinary body you love: a hand, a face, a child asleep. Christians say God came that close. If you pray, you can read verse fourteen once more, slowly, as your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Christmas. The feast of the birth of Jesus, when John's Gospel says the Word was made flesh and pitched his tent among us.
Your line: he dwelt among us. Today, look for the holy in something ordinary and close by: a meal, a voice, a face across the table. Day six hundred ninety-five.

screen: `DAY 695 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YEAR TWO CLOSE: THE BOOK IN YOUR HANDS.`

696.title: Year two close: the book in your hands
696.hook: a library you've walked through, from the garden to the shore at breakfast
696.howItsDone: Many Christians keep a favorite verse close, memorized, written in a Bible's margin or posted at home, and many churches mark the end of a season of reading with a time of looking back and giving thanks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Christmas and the Word made flesh, and your line was he dwelt among us. Where did you find the holy in something ordinary? Day six hundred ninety-six.

Picture the Bible as a building you've spent a year walking through. You came in through a garden, where God walked in the cool of the day. You crossed a desert with a whole people. You sat in a room full of songs, some joyful, some furious. You heard prophets shouting in the street. You walked with Jesus through Luke and through John, all the way to a charcoal fire on a beach at dawn, where the risen Jesus cooked breakfast for his friends. And this month, a few letters left on the table. Today is the last day of year two. Before you step outside, one look back, and one verse to take with you.
screen: `A GARDEN, A DESERT, A ROOM OF SONGS.`

segments.voice: Year two had seven parts. Genesis: beginnings, a garden, a flood, a family that kept going wrong and kept being carried. Exodus: slaves, a sea, manna, a mountain, a golden calf, and forty years in the wilderness. The Psalms and the wisdom books: prayers for every mood, and wisdom that knows life is short and good. The prophets: a burning coal, a potter, dry bones, a sulking prophet, a king on a donkey. Luke, read through: outsiders, meals and mercy. John, read through: the Word, the signs, the bread and the light and the good shepherd, and that breakfast on the shore. And three letters of joy, faith and love: Philippians, James and First John, with the elder's two short notes. Now the verse for today. Near the end of Deuteronomy, Moses gives his last speeches before the people cross into the land without him. He tells them the commandment isn't hidden away. It isn't up in heaven, where someone would have to climb and fetch it. It isn't across the sea, where someone would have to sail out and bring it back. In the King James Bible: "But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it." Very nigh. Near. The Hebrew word is karov: close by, within reach. Centuries later, Paul quoted this same line in his letter to the Romans: "The word is nigh thee, even in thy mouth, and in thy heart." Jews and Christians both treasure the verse and read it in their own ways. But the picture is shared: the word isn't a far-off mountain only experts can climb. After a year of reading, it's in your hands, and some of it is already in your mouth and your heart.
screen: `NOT IN HEAVEN, NOT ACROSS THE SEA.`
then, large: `THE WORD IS VERY NIGH UNTO THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write the one verse you'll keep. Settle, and breathe. Let the year go past like the rooms of that building: the garden, the desert, the songs, the prophets, the roads of Luke, the shore in John, the letters. Which verse stayed? Maybe the Lord is my shepherd. Maybe a line from a prophet, or no fear in love, or something small nobody else would pick. Don't choose the most famous one. Choose the one that's already near you, the one you catch yourself saying. After the bell, write it down by hand. If you pray, you can give thanks for a year of reading. The bell holds the time.
Year two close. The end of the book read in order: a library walked through, from the garden to the shore.

Your line: the word is near you. Today, put your verse where your hand will find it: a pocket, a wallet, a phone case. Tomorrow, year three begins with Joshua and the long story of Israel. Day six hundred ninety-six.
